title: 21 Creative Hobbies You Can Start at Your Kitchen Table, With the First Thing to Pick Up

body.text: Do you still make things with your hands? For a lot of adults the answer slipped from yes to no sometime after school art class, mostly because nobody asked for a drawing or a clay pot anymore.

Consider this your reason. Every hobby below works in a small apartment, at a kitchen table, after work. They're sorted by mess level, and many come with an easy first project, so you can pick the one that fits your space and your mood.
Low mess, low cost, and very easy to pack away. Great if you share a small space.

body.title: Junk journaling
body.note: Layer receipts, tickets and scraps into a notebook. It's part diary, part collage, and impossible to do wrong. Start with the [beginner's guide to junk journaling](/journal/how-to-start-junk-journaling), then the [supplies guide](/journal/junk-journaling-supplies-for-beginners) before you shop. **What makes it easier:** {{product:stationery-island-a5-blank-journal-180-pages|a blank journal}}, {{product:scotch-glue-stick-photo-safe-4-pack|a glue stick}} and {{product:mr-pen-washi-tape-21-rolls|washi tape}}, so the first page is a matter of gluing.

body.title: Scrapbooking
body.note: Print photos from one weekend and build a two-page spread around them. It's more structured than junk journaling, if you like a plan. **What makes it easier:** a scrapbook or photo album and {{product:scotch-glue-stick-photo-safe-4-pack|a photo-safe glue stick}}, so the two-page spread has somewhere to live.

body.title: Collage
body.note: Cut up old magazines and arrange images into postcards or a framed piece. It's surprisingly revealing about your taste. **What makes it easier:** sharp scissors and a glue stick, so edges stay clean and images stay where you put them.

body.title: Calligraphy and brush lettering
body.note: Brush pens and practice sheets are the whole kit. Drills are oddly soothing after a day of typing. **What makes it easier:** a set of brush pens, so thick and thin strokes come from one pen.

body.title: For a paper evening
body.dek: A journal, washi tape, an album or a brush pen is a small first buy that gets you to a finished page the same night.

body.text: A little more mess, still very manageable. Put down a tea towel and keep a jar of water handy.

body.title: Watercolor painting
body.note: No studio and no free Sunday needed. A little paint set, a sketchbook and twenty minutes at your kitchen table are enough, and the first time colors bleed into each other is a small thrill. [Watercolor painting for beginners](/journal/watercolor-painting-for-beginners) walks you through it. Try painting the flowers on your counter, your favorite mug, or whatever happens to be in front of you. **What makes it easier:** a small pan set and {{product:hapikalor-watercolor-pad-140lb-9x12|a pad of watercolor paper}}, so the first wash happens the evening the box arrives.

body.title: Paint by numbers
body.note: The no-pressure way to paint something frame-worthy. Ideal when you want to be creative but don't want to make a single decision. **What makes it easier:** a small paint-by-number kit with the numbered canvas, paints and a brush in one box; check the listing for what's included.

body.title: Painting thrifted frames and objects
body.note: Pick up a plain frame, vase or tray from a thrift store and give it stripes, checks or cherries with acrylics. Instant decor, very low risk. **What makes it easier:** a set of small acrylic craft paints and a flat brush, so stripes and checks go on in one sitting.
body.first: Paint a thrifted wooden frame with a simple checkerboard border.

body.caption: Twenty minutes, three colors, one jar of flowers.

body.title: For a painting evening
body.dek: A small paint set and a pad of paper, a paint-by-number kit or a few acrylics are enough for the first painting.

body.text: Clay and things you can hold

body.title: Air-dry clay
body.note: No wheel or kiln required, and [how to start air-dry clay](/journal/how-to-start-air-dry-clay) walks through a first project. Ring dishes, trinket trays and small ornaments air-dry at home (about a day to the touch for Crayola's, longer for thick pieces; check the label), then you can paint them. Keep finished pieces for display, not for food, drink or water. **What makes it easier:** a bucket of air-dry clay, a small set of clay tools and a work mat, so rolling, cutting and cleanup stay in one corner.

body.title: At-home pottery painting
body.note: Get a ceramic painting kit and follow its instructions. Treat painted pottery as display-only unless the kit or studio says it is food safe for your use. **What makes it easier:** a ceramic painting kit, so the pieces, paints and brushes arrive together; check the label for firing and use.

body.title: Jewelry making
body.note: Beads, wire and a pair of pliers. Make earrings to match an outfit or matching bracelets for friends.

body.title: Friendship bracelets
body.note: Quick, nostalgic and a natural fit for doing with friends. Letter beads make them yours. **What makes it easier:** a friendship bracelet kit, so the floss, beads and instructions arrive together. Check the label for small parts.

body.text: Portable, quiet and easy to do while watching something. If you like keeping your hands busy, start here.

body.title: Embroidery
body.note: A pre-printed design, a hoop and the right thread are all it takes. Learn three stitches and you're away; [how to start embroidery](/journal/how-to-start-embroidery) shows you how. **What makes it easier:** {{product:bradove-classic-embroidery-kit|a beginner embroidery kit}}, so the hoop, fabric and floss arrive together and the first evening is all stitching.

body.title: Cross-stitch
body.note: Little x-shaped stitches on gridded fabric following a chart. Very beginner-friendly and very satisfying to watch fill in. **What makes it easier:** a beginner kit with the chart, fabric and floss together, so you start on the first row, not the shopping.
body.first: Stitch a small motif from a beginner kit, like a strawberry or a star.

body.title: Punch needle
body.note: A tool that pushes loops of yarn through fabric. Makes fluffy, textured pieces fast, great for cushion covers and wall hangings.
body.first: Punch a small heart or flower on a 6-inch hoop.

body.title: Crochet
body.note: One hook, one ball of yarn. The first hour is fiddly; then it clicks. Granny squares first, bags and hats later. [How to start crocheting](/journal/how-to-start-crocheting) covers the first hour. **What makes it easier:** a few crochet hooks in different sizes and {{product:red-heart-super-saver-white-worsted|a ball of worsted yarn}}, so the first hour has the right size to hand.

body.title: Knitting
body.note: Two needles and very soothing rhythm. A coaster-sized square makes a satisfying first evening. **What makes it easier:** a pair of knitting needles and a ball of beginner yarn, so a coaster-sized square is one cast-on away.

body.title: Sewing a simple tote
body.note: A straight seam on a sewing machine (or by hand) gets you a tote bag in an afternoon. Look for a beginner pattern.
body.first: Sew a simple lined tote from a free beginner pattern.

body.title: For a thread-and-yarn evening
body.dek: A starter kit, a set of hooks or needles and a ball of beginner yarn keep your hands busy through a whole episode.

body.title: Flower arranging
body.note: One supermarket bunch, three jars. Learn about height and texture, then break every rule. Start with the [flower arranging guide](/journal/flower-arranging-as-a-hobby). **What makes it easier:** floral snips and a small vase, so stems cut cleanly and a supermarket bunch looks arranged.

body.title: Indoor gardening and propagation
body.note: A row of glass jars with pothos cuttings (cut just below a node) on a windowsill is a creative project and living decor. **What makes it easier:** a few propagation jars and a small pot, so a cutting has somewhere to sit by the window.

body.title: Baking and decorating
body.note: Cookie decorating is basically painting with icing. Practice on a Sunday and bring the results on Monday. **What makes it easier:** a cookie decorating kit with icing and sprinkles, so Sunday practice is all decorating.

body.title: For the living and edible hobbies
body.dek: Snips and a vase, a few jars, a decorating kit: small things that make a bunch of flowers, a cutting or a plate of cookies look arranged.

body.text: Paper hobbies are the easiest to begin with what you already have: old magazines, catalogs, receipts, gift wrap and an old notebook can carry you for weeks. Words need even less.

body.title: Creative writing
body.note: A notebook and a prompt. Write a tiny story set in the café you visited last weekend. Nobody has to read it. **What makes it easier:** {{product:stationery-island-a5-blank-journal-180-pages|a blank journal}} you like holding, so the prompt has somewhere to land.

body.text: Turn any of these into a craft night: pick one, set out supplies for four and add snacks. Clay, bracelets and cookie decorating are the easiest for groups.
How to start small and enjoy it more

items: **Pick one material**, not one of everything: paper, paint, clay or thread. If budget is on your mind, [15 hobbies to start this month](/journal/affordable-hobbies-under-25) shows the cheapest sensible way into each.
**Pick a single starter kit.** A kit puts everything in one box and removes decision fatigue, though [not every kit is worth it](/journal/creative-hobby-starter-kits-worth-considering).
**Give it three evenings** before you decide whether it's for you.
**Keep it visible.** A basket on the coffee table gets used; a box under the bed doesn't.
**Upgrade the thing you reach for most.** Once a hobby has stuck, a better brush, nicer paper or a basket for your supplies makes it even more fun.
